The program sets n to 2 and does switch (n). Case 2 has no break.

Follow the blue path on the left, top to bottom:
1. The switch jumps straight to the case label that matches n. That's case 2 on line 8. case 1 is skipped, never looked at again. puts("two") prints two.
2. There's no break after it. A case label is only a label, it doesn't stop execution. So control walks right past case 3: and runs puts("three"), which prints three. That red stretch is the fallthrough.
3. The break on line 12 ends the switch. case 4 never runs.
4. After the switch, puts("done") prints done.

Real output from the run (Apple clang, C17, run twice):
two
three
done

The right panel is with_break.c, which adds a break after case 1 and after case 2. Same n = 2, and it prints only two from the switch, then done.

The rule in one line: a case label only marks where execution enters a switch; it never ends a case. Once inside, you keep running until a break, or until the end of the switch body.

The two usual wrong guesses: that the next label stops it (that would print two, done), or that fallthrough runs all the way to the last case (two, three, four, done). The break on line 12 is what stops it before case 4.

Side note: gcc-16 with -Wextra warns that lines 7 and 9 may fall through. Apple clang with -Wextra says nothing for this program.
